**Why a geometric quotient is categorical.** Let $\pi:X\to Y$ satisfy (i)–(iii)
and let $f:X\to Z$ be a $G$-invariant morphism to a classical variety $Z$. By
(i) two points of a fibre of $\pi$ lie in one orbit, on which $f$ is constant,
so $f$ factors through a unique set map $\bar f:Y\to Z$. For $W\subseteq Z$
open, $\pi^{-1}(\bar f^{-1}(W))=f^{-1}(W)$ is open in $X$ by continuity of $f$,
so $\bar f^{-1}(W)$ is open in $Y$ by (ii): $\bar f$ is continuous. If $V$ is an
affine chart of $Z$ with coordinates $s$ and $U:=\bar f^{-1}(V)$, then
$s\circ f$ is a $G$-invariant regular function on $\pi^{-1}(U)$, hence by (iii)
is the pullback along $\pi$ of a unique regular function on $U$; that function
is $s\circ\bar f$. Since this holds for every coordinate $s$ of an affine chart,
$\bar f$ is a morphism
([[def-classical-affine-variety-morphism]],
[[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]), and local
agreement of the resulting morphisms on overlapping charts gives a morphism
$Y\to Z$. Surjectivity in (i) makes the factorisation unique. If also
$\pi':X\to Y'$ is a categorical quotient, the universal property applied to
$\pi'$ and to $\pi$ yields morphisms $\varphi:Y\to Y'$ with $\varphi\pi=\pi'$
and $\psi:Y'\to Y$ with $\psi\pi'=\pi$; then $(\varphi\psi)\pi'=\pi'$ and
$(\psi\varphi)\pi=\pi$, so uniqueness of the factorisation of $\pi'$ through
$\pi'$ and of $\pi$ through $\pi$ forces $\varphi\psi=\operatorname{id}_{Y'}$
and $\psi\varphi=\operatorname{id}_Y$. Thus categorical and geometric
quotients are unique up to unique isomorphism, and for a geometric quotient
(i)–(ii) say exactly that the underlying map is the quotient map of the orbit
equivalence relation with the quotient topology.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a scheme of finite type over $\mathbb C$
and let $x\in X$ be a closed point with residue field $\mathbb C$. Choose an
affine neighborhood of $x$ presented as (adding a dummy coordinate if needed)
$\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb C[w_1,\ldots,w_n]/I)$, with $n\ge1$, $I$ a
finitely generated polynomial ideal contained in $(w_1,\ldots,w_n)$, and $x$
the origin. Write
$A=(\mathbb C[w_1,\ldots,w_n]_{(w_1,\ldots,w_n)})/I\mathbb C[w_1,\ldots,w_n]_{(w_1,\ldots,w_n)}$.
On this chart, define the analytic local ring by extending the same ideal to
holomorphic germs,
$B=\mathbb C\{w_1,\ldots,w_n\}/I\mathbb C\{w_1,\ldots,w_n\}$; this quotient
retains the given scheme structure, including nilpotents. For a local ring $R$
with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_R$, let
$\widehat R=\varprojlim_{k\ge1}R/\mathfrak m_R^k$.

The canonical local homomorphism $A\to B$, which sends each polynomial class
to the same holomorphic germ, is injective and faithfully flat.
Its induced map $\widehat A\to\widehat B$ is an isomorphism, with both
completions canonically identified with
$\mathbb C\llbracket w_1,\ldots,w_n\rrbracket/I\mathbb C\llbracket w_1,\ldots,w_n\rrbracket$. For every
$A$-module $M$, the map $M\to M\otimes_A B$ is injective, and the quotient
$B/A$ is a flat $A$-module. These are local-ring conclusions; no relative
direct-image comparison is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional complex manifold and let $\mathcal O_M$ be its sheaf of holomorphic functions. For every open $U\subseteq M$ and every finite tuple $f_1,\ldots,f_q\in\mathcal O_M(U)$, the relation sheaf
$$
\ker\!\left(\mathcal O_U^{\oplus q}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_U,\quad(a_1,\ldots,a_q)\longmapsto\sum_{j=1}^q a_jf_j\right)
$$
is locally of finite type: every point has a neighborhood on which one finite family of relation sections generates the relation stalk at every point. Consequently $\mathcal O_M$ is coherent. Coherent $\mathcal O_M$-module sheaves are closed under kernels, cokernels, and finite extensions. For every coherent $\mathcal O_M$-module $\mathcal F$, point $x\in M$, and finite integer $\ell\ge0$, there are a chart neighborhood $W$ of $x$ and finite ranks $p_0,\ldots,p_\ell$ for which
$$
\mathcal O_W^{\oplus p_\ell}\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow\mathcal O_W^{\oplus p_0}\longrightarrow\mathcal F|_W\longrightarrow0
$$
is exact at $\mathcal F|_W$ and at every free term except the leftmost one. No exactness at the leftmost free term and no global analytic free resolution are asserted.

For its topology, a coordinate polydisc means the image in a holomorphic chart of a product of open coordinate discs. Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $r\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, let
$X=\mathbb P^r(\mathbb C)=(\mathbb C^{r+1}\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb C^\times$
with its standard quotient complex-manifold structure, and let $E\to X$ be a
holomorphic vector bundle of finite rank.
Write $\mathcal O(E)$ for its sheaf of holomorphic sections, and let
$H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ denote the $q$th right-derived global-sections group of an
abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $X$. For
$0\le q\le r$, let $\mathcal A^{0,q}(E)$ be the sheaf of smooth sections of
$\Lambda^{0,q}T^*X\otimes_{\mathbb C}E$, where $\Lambda^{0,q}T^*X$ is the
$q$th exterior power of the antiholomorphic cotangent subbundle. In a
holomorphic local frame of $E$,
define $\bar\partial_E$ by applying the scalar $\bar\partial$ to each
coefficient form; holomorphic transition matrices make this definition
independent of frame, and $\bar\partial_E^2=0$. Set
$\mathcal A^{0,q}(E)=0$ for $q>r$ and define
$$H^q_{\bar\partial}(X,E):=\frac{\ker\bigl(\bar\partial_E:\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{0,q}(E))\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{0,q+1}(E))\bigr)}{\operatorname{im}\bigl(\bar\partial_E:\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{0,q-1}(E))\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{0,q}(E))\bigr)},$$
where $\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$ denotes the group of sections of $\mathcal F$ over
$X$ and the denominator is zero for $q=0$. For every $q\ge0$, the canonical
comparison induced by the smooth Dolbeault resolution is an isomorphism
$$H^q(X,\mathcal O(E))\cong H^q_{\bar\partial}(X,E).$$
For the trivial line bundle $E=\mathcal O_X$ and $0\le r\le3$, this gives
$$H^0(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=\mathbb C,\qquad H^q(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=0\quad(q>0).$$
The scalar cohomology conclusion is obtained by the direct Laurent–Čech
calculation on the standard projective cover; no GAGA theorem, Kähler Hodge
theorem in dimensions above one, or arbitrary-coherent projective vanishing is
assumed.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$\mathcal O(d)=\widetilde{S(d)}$, and let $F$ be a coherent
$\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^n_k}$-module. Then there is a finitely generated graded
$S$-module $M$ with $\widetilde M\cong F$ and an exact sequence of graded
$S$-modules with degree-preserving maps
$$0\longrightarrow F_{n+1}\longrightarrow F_n\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow F_0\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow 0$$
in which every $F_i$ is a finite direct sum of shifted free modules $S(d)$
with $d\in\mathbb Z$, and whose sheafification
$$0\longrightarrow\widetilde F_{n+1}\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow\widetilde F_0\longrightarrow F\longrightarrow 0$$
is an exact sequence of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^n_k}$-modules in which every
$\widetilde F_i$ is a finite direct sum $\bigoplus_j\mathcal O(d_{ij})$ of
twisting sheaves. The resolution has length at most $n+1$: the displayed free
terms $F_0,\dots,F_{n+1}$ are finite direct sums of shifted free modules, any
of them may be zero, a shorter resolution is allowed when it terminates
earlier, and the truncation degree of $M$ is chosen so that $M$ is finitely
generated and $\widetilde M\cong F$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a commutative
ring with $1$ ([[def-commutative-ring]]), let $n\ge0$, let $d\in\mathbb Z$ and
let $X=\mathbb P^n_A\cong\operatorname{Proj}A[x_0,\dots,x_n]$ be relative
projective space ([[def-relative-projective-space-standard-charts]],
[[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]]), with twisting sheaf
$\mathcal O_X(d)$ ([[def-twisting-sheaf-proj]]) and cohomology
$H^q(X,\mathcal O_X(d))$. Then
$$H^q(X,\mathcal O_X(d))=0\qquad\text{unless }q=0\text{ or }q=n.$$
If $n>0$, then $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))\cong A[x_0,\dots,x_n]_d$ when $d\ge0$
and $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))=0$ when $d<0$, where
$A[x_0,\dots,x_n]_d$ is the degree-$d$ graded piece
([[def-graded-ring-and-graded-module]]); and $H^n(X,\mathcal O_X(d))$ is the
free $A$-module on the Laurent monomials $x_0^{e_0}\cdots x_n^{e_n}$ with
$e_i<0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_ie_i=d$, so that it is nonzero precisely when
$d\le-n-1$ and $A\ne0$. For $n=0$ one has $\mathbb P^0_A=\operatorname{Spec}A$
and $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))\cong A$ for every $d\in\mathbb Z$, with all higher
groups zero. The zero ring $A=0$ is allowed: then $X=\varnothing$ and all
groups are zero, in agreement with both displayed descriptions.

H-projective convention ([[def-projective-morphism-pre-proj]]): the structure
morphism $X\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ factors as a closed immersion
$X\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_A$ followed by the projection, for some $N\ge0$
([[def-relative-projective-space-standard-charts]]). Let $L$ be an ample
invertible $\mathcal O_X$-module ([[def-ample-invertible-sheaf]],
[[def-invertible-sheaf]]) and let $\mathcal F$ be a coherent
$\mathcal O_X$-module ([[def-coherent-module-scheme]]). Then there is an
integer $m_0$ such that
$$H^q\bigl(X,\mathcal F\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}L^{\otimes m}\bigr)=0$$
for every $q>0$ and every integer $m\ge m_0$, with a single bound $m_0$
working simultaneously for all $q$; here $H^q$ is sheaf cohomology
([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]) and $L^{\otimes m}$ is the
$m$-fold tensor power ([[def-twist-quasi-coherent-sheaf-projective]]). The
empty scheme $X$, the empty base $\operatorname{Spec}A=\varnothing$, the zero
ring $A=0$, the zero module $\mathcal F=0$ and the case of an ample $L$ with
$\mathcal O(1)$ already very ample for a power $L^{\otimes d}$ with $d=1$ are
included. No effectivity of $m_0$ is claimed.

Let
$$\cdots \to A_{n-1} \to A_n \to A_{n+1} \to A_{n+2} \to A_{n+3} \to \cdots$$
and
$$\cdots \to B_{n-1} \to B_n \to B_{n+1} \to B_{n+2} \to B_{n+3} \to \cdots$$
be long exact sequences in an abelian category, together with a morphism of
these sequences. If the four comparison maps at $A_{n-1},A_n,A_{n+2},A_{n+3}$
are isomorphisms, then the comparison map $A_{n+1} \to B_{n+1}$ is an
isomorphism.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, and let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a ringed space. Then
the abelian category $\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$ of $\mathcal O_X$-modules has
enough injectives: every $\mathcal O_X$-module embeds into an injective
$\mathcal O_X$-module, and the functorial injective embedding supplied by the
Grothendieck injective-embedding theorem for Grothendieck categories supplies,
by iteration of cokernels, one specific injective resolution
$$0\to\mathcal F\to I^0(\mathcal F)\to I^1(\mathcal F)\to\cdots$$
to each $\mathcal O_X$-module $\mathcal F$ with no further selection
([[def-injective-resolution-in-an-abelian-category]]). The Axiom of Choice
enters exactly through that embedding theorem applied to
$\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$; the category-theoretic verification below is
choice-free.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $X$ be a topological space and let
$\mathcal F$ be a flasque sheaf of abelian groups on $X$
([[def-flasque-sheaf]]). Then for every open subspace $U\subseteq X$ and every
integer $q>0$,
$$H^q(U,\mathcal F|_U)=0,$$
where $H^q(U,-)$ denotes sheaf cohomology on the space $U$
([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]) computed with the global
sections functor of $U$, and $\mathcal F|_U$ is the restriction of $\mathcal F$
to $U$. Equivalently, every restriction $\mathcal F|_U$ is $\Gamma$-acyclic
([[def-acyclic-sheaf-global-sections]]).

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice.

Let $I$ be a supplied injective resolution datum on a class $\mathcal D$, let
$F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ be an additive left exact functor, and let
$$0\to A\to J^0\to J^1\to J^2\to\cdots$$
be an $F$-acyclic resolution of $A$ relative to $I$. Assume moreover that
$A\in\mathcal D$ and that, for $Z^0:=A$ and
$$0\to Z^q\to J^q\to Z^{q+1}\to0\qquad(q\ge0),$$
each $Z^q$ lies in $\mathcal D$. Then for every $n\ge 0$ there is a canonical
isomorphism
$$R_I^nF(A)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^n(F(J^\bullet_{\mathrm{del}})).$$

Let $\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ be a morphism of sheaves of sets on a
topological space $X$, and let $I$ be the **presheaf image**
$$I(U):=\varphi_U(\mathcal F(U))\subseteq\mathcal G(U).$$
Define the **image sheaf** $J$ by
$$ J(U):=\left\{\,t\in\mathcal G(U): \text{ for every }x\in U\text{ there exists }x\in V\subseteq U \text{ and }s\in\mathcal F(V)\text{ with }\varphi_V(s)=t|_V\,\right\}. $$
Then $J$ is a subsheaf of $\mathcal G$, $\varphi$ factors through $J$, and the
canonical map
$$aI\longrightarrow J$$
is an isomorphism. In particular, the image sheaf is the sheafification of the
objectwise image presheaf.

Let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf on a topological space $X$, let
$\eta_{\mathcal F}:\mathcal F\to a\mathcal F$ be its sheafification map, and let
$\mathcal G$ be a sheaf on $X$. Then every morphism of presheaves
$$\varphi:\mathcal F\longrightarrow\mathcal G$$
factors uniquely through $\eta_{\mathcal F}$:
there is a unique morphism of sheaves
$$\overline\varphi:a\mathcal F\longrightarrow\mathcal G$$
such that
$$\varphi=\overline\varphi\circ\eta_{\mathcal F}.$$

Let $(f,f^\sharp):(X,\mathcal O_X)\to(Y,\mathcal O_Y)$ be a morphism of ringed
spaces and let $\mathcal F$ be an $\mathcal O_X$-module
([[def-module-on-ringed-space]]). The direct image presheaf
$f_*\mathcal F$ is defined on opens $V\subseteq Y$ by
$(f_*\mathcal F)(V)=\mathcal F(f^{-1}(V))$
([[def-direct-image-sheaf]]); when $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf of modules, this
presheaf is again a sheaf of modules on $Y$
([[lem-direct-image-is-sheaf]]), and for a morphism of ringed spaces it is an
$\mathcal O_Y$-module, because $f_*$ is right adjoint to the inverse image
functor $f^*$ on modules ([[thm-pullback-pushforward-module-adjunction]]); a
right adjoint is left exact and additive
([[cor-a-right-adjoint-is-left-exact-and-a-left-adjoint-is-right-exact]]).

Fix the supplied functorial injective resolution datum $I$ on
$\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$ of
[[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]: it assigns to every
$\mathcal O_X$-module $\mathcal F$ one specific injective resolution
$0\to\mathcal F\to I^0(\mathcal F)\to I^1(\mathcal F)\to\cdots$
([[def-injective-resolution-in-an-abelian-category]]) with deleted complex
$I(\mathcal F)_{\mathrm{del}}$
([[def-right-derived-object-relative-to-injective-resolution-data]]). For
every $q\in\mathbb Z$ define the **$q$-th higher direct image sheaf**

$$R^qf_*\mathcal F:=R_I^qf_*(\mathcal F)=H^q\bigl(f_*I(\mathcal F)_{\mathrm{del}}\bigr),$$

the $q$-th right derived object of the additive left exact functor
$f_*:\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)\to\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_Y)$ relative to the
fixed datum $I$ ([[def-right-derived-object-relative-to-injective-resolution-data]]),
the cohomology object being taken in the abelian category of
$\mathcal O_Y$-modules. We also keep the convention $R^qf_*\mathcal F=0$ for
$q<0$.

By the derived-object convention this makes $R^qf_*\mathcal F$ a specific
$\mathcal O_Y$-module for every $\mathcal F$ and $q$, depending on the fixed
datum $I$; in degree zero the left exactness of $f_*$ supplies a canonical
natural isomorphism $R^0f_*\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\sim}f_*\mathcal F$
([[thm-zero-th-right-derived-functor-of-a-left-exact-functor-recovers-the-functor]],
which assumes the Axiom of Dependent Choice
([[def-dependent-choice]])), so the $q=0$ term is the ordinary direct image.
The Axiom of Choice supplies the functorial injective resolution datum of
$\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$ ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and implies the
Dependent Choice required by the cited degree-zero and comparison theorems
([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]). If $J$ is any other supplied injective resolution
datum on $\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$, then the functors $R_I^qf_*$ and
$R_J^qf_*$ are naturally isomorphic
([[thm-right-derived-functors-from-two-supplied-injective-resolution-data-are-naturally-isomorphic]]),
so the higher direct image is independent of the resolution up to a canonical
comparison isomorphism.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $X$ be a topological space with supplied
functorial injective resolution datum $I_X$ and sheaf cohomology
$H^q(X,-)$ as in [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]].

1. (Covariance in the sheaf.) Every morphism $\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$
   of abelian sheaves on $X$ induces additive maps
   $H^q(X,\varphi):H^q(X,\mathcal F)\to H^q(X,\mathcal G)$, and
   $\mathcal F\mapsto H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ is a covariant additive functor.
2. (Contravariance in the space.) Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, let
   $\mathcal G$ be an abelian sheaf on $Y$, let $\mathcal F$ be an abelian sheaf on $X$, and let
   $\varphi:f^{-1}\mathcal G\to\mathcal F$ be a morphism of abelian sheaves. Then there are maps
   $$H^q(Y,\mathcal G)\longrightarrow H^q(X,\mathcal F)\qquad(q\ge0)$$
   depending only on $\varphi$, natural in $\mathcal G$ and $\mathcal F$, and in
   degree $0$ the map is the composite
   $\Gamma(Y,\mathcal G)\to\Gamma(X,f^{-1}\mathcal G)\xrightarrow{\ \Gamma(X,\varphi)\ }\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$
   of section pullback with $\varphi$; for composable data
   $g:Y\to Z$, $\psi:g^{-1}\mathcal H\to\mathcal G$,
   $\varphi:f^{-1}\mathcal G\to\mathcal F$ the map of the composite pair
   $\varphi\circ f^{-1}\psi:(gf)^{-1}\mathcal H\to\mathcal F$ is the composite of
   the two maps (compatibility with compositions).

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $I \trianglelefteq R$ satisfy $I \subseteq J(R)$, and let $M$ be a finitely generated left $R$-module. If $IM=M$, then $M=0$.
The field $\mathbb C$ is algebraically closed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a commutative
ring and let $n\ge0$ be an integer, and let $\mathbb P^n_A$ be the projective
space over $A$ with its standard charts
([[def-relative-projective-space-standard-charts]]). Then every
quasi-coherent $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^n_A}$-module $\mathcal F$
([[def-quasi-coherent-module-scheme]]) satisfies
$$H^q(\mathbb P^n_A,\mathcal F)=0$$
for every integer $q>n$, where $H^q$ is sheaf cohomology
([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]) applied to the underlying
sheaf of abelian groups of $\mathcal F$ ([[def-module-on-ringed-space]]). The
case $n=0$ is included; the zero ring $A=0$ is allowed, and then
$\mathbb P^n_A=\varnothing$.

derivations.claim: At a complex point, coherent algebraic and analytic modules are finite-dimensional complex vector spaces, so the absolute assertions hold in dimension zero. Flatness in [A1] makes analytification exact stalkwise, including for nonreduced finite-type schemes. Tensor associativity gives tensor compatibility and compatibility with quotient restriction to a hyperplane. A finite algebraic presentation analytifies to a finite analytic presentation, so [A3] ensures its cokernel is coherent. For a closed analytic embedding, direct image is exact on stalks and preserves flabby sheaves: its sections over an open are the original sections over the intersection with the closed subspace. Pushing forward a flabby resolution therefore identifies cohomology on the closed subspace and its direct image. These facts apply to the hyperplane sequences below.

Suppose the absolute theorem has been proved in dimensions below $r$, where $1\le r\le3$. For $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}$ the natural comparison is an isomorphism by [A5] and [F3]. The exact hyperplane sequences $0\to\mathcal O(m-1)\xrightarrow{x_0}\mathcal O(m)\to i_*\mathcal O_H(m)\to0$ exist on both sides by step 1.1, and their cohomology maps commute with analytification. For $m\ge1$, assume comparison at $m-1$. The lower-dimensional comparison and [F3] give $H^q(H,\mathcal O_H(m))=0$ for $q>0$; the sequence therefore gives analytic higher vanishing at $m$ and an exact sequence on global sections. Every homogeneous degree-$m$ polynomial on $H$ extends by the same polynomial in $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ on $\mathbb P^r$; the kernel of restriction is $x_0$ times the degree-$m-1$ polynomials. The natural map of these exact section sequences is an isomorphism at its outer terms, hence also at its middle term by [F4]. This proves the natural comparison for all $m\ge0$ without using GAGA in dimension $r$.

For the negative twists, the sequence $0\to\mathcal O(-1)\to\mathcal O\to i_*\mathcal O_H\to0$ has restriction $\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ equal to the identity in degree zero and no positive cohomology in the two right terms by [A5] and lower-dimensional comparison. Thus analytic $\mathcal O(-1)$ is acyclic, as is its algebraic counterpart by [F3]. For every $m<-1$, multiplication by a power of $x_0$ injects the line bundle $\mathcal O(m)$ into $\mathcal O(-1)$: in each analytic chart its local equation is a nonzero holomorphic function in the integral holomorphic germ ring, so multiplication is injective. Hence $H^0(\mathcal O(m))=0$. Descend using $0\to\mathcal O(m)\to\mathcal O(m+1)\to i_*\mathcal O_H(m+1)\to0$. Comparison is already known at $m+1$ and on the hyperplane at every twist. For $q\ge1$, the four neighbors in $H^{q-1}(\mathcal O(m+1))\to H^{q-1}(\mathcal O_H(m+1))\to H^q(\mathcal O(m))\to H^q(\mathcal O(m+1))\to H^q(\mathcal O_H(m+1))$ are therefore naturally compared isomorphically, so [F4] gives the middle comparison. This also handles $r=1$, where the point hyperplane's negative twists still have a one-dimensional section space; they were not incorrectly set to zero. Thus all integer twists have canonical cohomology comparison, without analytic Serre duality or an affine finite-pole assertion.

Resolve an algebraic coherent $\mathcal F$ by [F2]. Its finite twisting-sheaf resolution stays exact analytically by step 1.1. Starting at its leftmost term, the long exact sequences and steps 2.1 and 3.1 prove cohomology comparison for each successive cokernel and hence for $\mathcal F$ in every degree. This uses the actual finite resolution, not an unproved global analytic free resolution.

Let $\mathcal M$ now be any coherent analytic sheaf on $\mathbb P^r$. For every nonzero linear section $s$, retain both $K_s=\ker(\mathcal M(-1)\xrightarrow{s}\mathcal M)$ and $Q_s=\operatorname{coker}(s)$, and write $I_s=\operatorname{im}(s)$. Locally $s$ is a hyperplane equation, so it annihilates $K_s$ and $Q_s$; [A3] makes them coherent sheaves on $H_s\cong\mathbb P^{r-1}$. The inductive equivalence algebraizes them. By [F3], their positive cohomology vanishes after sufficiently positive twists. The two exact sequences $0\to K_s(n)\to\mathcal M(n-1)\to I_s(n)\to0$ and $0\to I_s(n)\to\mathcal M(n)\to Q_s(n)\to0$ then show that multiplication by $s$ on $H^q(\mathcal M(n-1))$ is eventually an isomorphism for $q\ge2$, and eventually surjective for $q=1$. The $H^0(Q_s(n))$ term prevents an initial claim of injectivity in degree one. This argument includes hyperplane torsion; $s$ was not assumed injective on $\mathcal M$.

For finitely presented algebraic $\mathcal F$, a finite presentation computes the sheaf $\mathcal H om(\mathcal F,\mathcal G)$ as a kernel between finite powers of $\mathcal G$. Exact analytification and [A3] therefore identify its analytification with analytic $\mathcal H om(\mathcal F^{an},\mathcal G^{an})$. Step 4.1 in degree zero identifies morphisms. A finite locally free resolution of $\mathcal F$ computes global $\operatorname{Ext}^q$ by the hypercohomology of its Hom complex: locally free Hom is exact, and an injective resolution gives the resulting double-complex comparison. Termwise cohomology comparison and finiteness of the resolution identify algebraic and analytic Ext in every degree. Thus full faithfulness and cohomology/Ext comparison in dimension $r$ are proved before essential surjectivity.

Fix $q>0$ and a nonzero $s_0$. For $q=1$, the eventual surjections in step 4.2 make the finite dimensions in [A4] nonincreasing integers, hence eventually constant; thereafter multiplication by $s_0$ is an isomorphism. For $q\ge2$ it is already eventually an isomorphism. Choose $N$ beyond this range, put $V=H^q(\mathcal M(N))$, and identify each $H^q(\mathcal M(n))$, $n\ge N$, with $V$ by successive multiplication by $s_0$. A second independent section $s_1$ induces an endomorphism $T_n$ on $V$ between successive degrees. The commuting multiplication square gives $T_{n+1}=T_n=T$. If $V\ne0$, choose an eigenvalue $\lambda$ by [F7]. Multiplication by the nonzero section $s_1-\lambda s_0$ then induces $T-\lambda I$, singular at every such degree. But step 4.2 applied to this fixed section is eventually an isomorphism for $q\ge2$; for $q=1$ it is eventually surjective between spaces of the same stabilized dimension and hence an isomorphism too. This contradiction proves eventual vanishing. The eigenvalue is chosen before its section's threshold; no bound uniform over an infinite pencil is used.

A simultaneous bound is available. For $1\le q\le r$ take the maximum of the finitely many bounds from step 5.2. If $q>r$, the inductive algebraic dimension bound [F7] makes all relevant cohomology groups of $K_s,Q_s$ in step 4.2 zero at every twist. Multiplication by every nonzero $s$ is then an isomorphism on $H^q(\mathcal M(n))$ at every integer $n$. The same two-section contradiction starting at any degree forces these groups to be zero at every twist. Thus one integer bounds vanishing for all $q>0$.

Fix a point $p$ and choose a hyperplane $H_s$ through it. By the inductive equivalence, $Q_s$ is algebraic. Its finite resolution [F2] begins with a surjection from a finite sum of twisting sheaves. After a sufficiently positive twist each summand is generated by its finite homogeneous monomials, so $Q_s(n)$ has finitely many global generators, analytically as well by inductive comparison. Also choose $n$ so $H^1(\mathcal M(n-1))=0$ by step 6.1 and $H^2(K_s(n))=0$ by induction and [F3]. The first exact sequence in step 4.2 gives $H^1(I_s(n))=0$; the second then lifts those finitely many generators to global sections of $\mathcal M(n)$. The cokernel $C$ of these lifts satisfies $C_p/sC_p=0$, so local Nakayama [F7] gives $C_p=0$. Finite local generation of the coherent cokernel gives an open neighborhood of $p$ on which the lifts generate.

Shrink each such neighborhood into a coordinate nonvanishing set $\{\ell_p\ne0\}$, with generating sections of some twist $n_p$. Compactness gives finitely many neighborhoods $U_j$ covering projective space, with integers $n_j$. For every $n\ge\max_j n_j$, multiply the $j$th generating set by $\ell_j^{n-n_j}$. These are global sections of $\mathcal M(n)$ and still generate on $U_j$, since $\ell_j$ is a unit there. Their finite union generates everywhere. This proves analytic positive-twist generation from the exact earlier suppliers. No assertion about finite pole order of arbitrary entire functions on an affine chart is used.

Apply step 8.1 to $\mathcal M$ to obtain a surjection $\mathcal O(-a)^u\to\mathcal M$. Its kernel is coherent by [A3]. Choose the second generator twist $b\ge a$ large enough for step 8.1 to give a surjection $\mathcal O(-b)^v$ onto that kernel. This gives a finite presentation $\mathcal O(-b)^v\to\mathcal O(-a)^u\to\mathcal M\to0$. Every matrix entry is a holomorphic section of $\mathcal O(b-a)$, with $b-a\ge0$, so step 2.1 identifies it with an algebraic section. More generally step 3.1 supplies the same comparison at every negative twist. Take its algebraic cokernel; step 1.1 identifies its analytification with $\mathcal M$. Step 5.1 algebraizes each isomorphism and its inverse and preserves their identity composites. This proves essential surjectivity and completes the absolute induction through dimensions $0,1,2,3$, including the claimed dimensions two and three.

To complete the family comparison after the absolute equivalence of step 9.1, first establish the local-section formula: for any morphism of ringed spaces $f:Y\to B$ and module sheaf $M$, take the module-injective resolution from [F5]. Each term is flasque, its restriction to $f^{-1}U$ is flasque for every open $U\subset B$, and hence its sections there compute $H^q(f^{-1}U,M)$ by the acyclic-resolution theorem. The cohomology sheaf of $f_*I^\bullet$ is the sheafification of its presheaf cohomology: kernels are computed on opens, image sheaves are the sheafifications of presheaf images, and the assertion follows on stalks by exactness of filtered colimits. Thus $R^qf_*M=(U\mapsto H^q(f^{-1}U,M))^\#$, compatibly with restrictions and scalar multiplication. This argument covers analytic ringed spaces as well as schemes.

Write $Y=X\times S$ and let $\eta_Y:Y^{an}\to Y$, $\eta_S:S^{an}\to S$ be analytification maps. For every algebraic open $U\subset S$, [F6] gives $H^q(p^{-1}U,\mathcal E)\to H^q((p^{an})^{-1}\eta_S^{-1}U,\mathcal E^{an})$. Composing with the presheaf-to-sheaf map of step 10.1, then sheafifying on $S$, gives the $\mathcal O_S$-linear map $R^qp_*\mathcal E\to\eta_{S*}R^qp^{an}_*\mathcal E^{an}$. Pull back and tensor with $\mathcal O_{S^{an}}$ to obtain $c_q:(R^qp_*\mathcal E)^{an}\to R^qp^{an}_*\mathcal E^{an}$; explicitly $a\otimes[\xi]$ maps to $a$ times the analytically pulled-back germ of $\xi$. Tensor balancing proves well-definedness. This constructs an actual comparison morphism without assuming its invertibility or a relative-GAGA theorem.

At $t\in S^{an}$ over the closed complex point $s\in S$, tensor associativity gives $(M^{an})(t)=M(s)$ for every algebraic module sheaf $M$, and $\mathcal E^{an}|_{X^{an}\times\{t\}}=(\mathcal E_s)^{an}$. These are underived restrictions, valid also for singular or nonreduced bases. The square with top map $c_q(t)$, vertical maps the assumed algebraic and analytic fiber-base-change maps, and bottom map $H^q(X,\mathcal E_s)\to H^q(X^{an},(\mathcal E_s)^{an})$ commutes: represent a stalk by a class on $p^{-1}U$ using step 10.1; both paths pull back that class along the same map from the analytic fiber, with identical tensor restriction of coefficients, so [F6] identifies them. The bottom map is an isomorphism by step 4.1, and both vertical maps are isomorphisms by the Statement's explicit hypotheses. Hence $c_q(t)$ is an isomorphism. Both sheaves compared by $c_q$ are finite locally free by those same hypotheses. Locally their ranks agree, and its matrix has determinant with nonzero residue at every $t$, hence a unit; the adjugate gives a local inverse. Therefore $c_q$ is an isomorphism.

For an algebraic finite-type base map $S'\to S$, apply the same class-pullback construction to the pulled-back family. Tensor associativity identifies its analytification with the analytic pullback family. The square of the two comparison morphisms and the algebraic and analytic base-change maps commutes, since all maps pull back the same local cohomology classes and [F6] respects compositions. Whenever both families satisfy the Statement's locally-free and fiber-base-change hypotheses, step 12.1 makes their comparison morphisms invertible, so it identifies their base-change maps. This proves the complete stated family range, including the closed-fiber maps, without asserting arbitrary analytic-family algebraization. Full AC is inherited through [F1] and the resolution construction [F5]. The exact analytic suppliers [A1], [A3]–[A5] remain prerequisite proof obligations until their actual carriers are checked; the internal Serre argument above does not certify them.

citations.quote: For $n=2$ or $3$, let $X=\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}$ and let $X^{an}$ be its complex analytic space and $\eta:X^{an}\to X$ the canonical morphism of ringed spaces. Define analytification on $X^{an}$ by $\mathcal F^{an}=\eta^{-1}\mathcal F\otimes_{\eta^{-1}\mathcal O_X}\mathcal O_{X^{an}}$. It is an exact tensor-compatible equivalence from algebraic coherent sheaves (locally finitely presented $\mathcal O_X$-modules) to holomorphic coherent sheaves. It identifies algebraic and holomorphic morphisms, preserves cohomology and the derived morphism groups $\operatorname{Ext}^q$, and commutes with restriction to the fixed hyperplane $L_\infty=\{z_0=0\}$. For an algebraic coherent sheaf $\mathcal E$ flat over a finite-type complex parameter scheme $S$, let $p:X\times S\to S$ be projection. Analytification commutes with the algebraic family structure and fiber restrictions. Whenever the algebraic and analytic higher direct images $R^qp_*\mathcal E$ are locally free and the natural maps from their residue-field fibers to $H^q(X_s,\mathcal E_s)$ are isomorphisms, the comparison identifies those direct images and base-change maps. No assertion is made that an arbitrary holomorphic family over a nonproper algebraic base algebraizes.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) inherited from the finite
coherent-resolution and cohomological suppliers. A section $s$ of a rank-$d$
bundle $Q$ is a **regular section** here if, at each point of its zero scheme
$Z(s)$, some local frame expresses $s$ by $d$ components forming a regular
sequence of length $d$ in the local ring. Under this hypothesis it has exact
Koszul resolution
$\bigwedge^dQ^\vee\to\cdots\to Q^\vee\to\mathcal O\to\mathcal O_{Z(s)}\to0$.
Tensoring with a vector bundle preserves it. If a coherent sheaf $H$ has a
finite locally free resolution on a scheme and $t$ is a Cartier equation acting
injectively on $H$, restricting the resolution to $t=0$ remains exact and
resolves $H/tH$. In the deformation blowup for a closed embedding of smooth
quasi-projective varieties $i:X\hookrightarrow Y$, let $E$ be a finite
locally free sheaf on $X$. The strict transform
$F:X\times\mathbb P^1\hookrightarrow M$ is disjoint from
$B=\operatorname{Bl}_XY$, and a resolution of $F_*\operatorname{pr}_X^*E$
restricts exactly to the ordinary $Y$ fibre and to
$P=\mathbb P_{\mathrm{lines}}(N\oplus1)$; on $B$ it is an exact complex.

For an additive left-exact functor $F$ and a bounded-below complex $K$ with supplied Cartan–Eilenberg resolution $I$, there is a spectral sequence
$$E_1^{p,q}=R^qF(K^p)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathbb R_I^{p+q}F(K),\qquad d_r:(p,q)\mapsto(p+r,q-r+1).$$
Here $q\ge0$ and $p\ge b$ if $K^p=0$ for $p<b$. It is first quadrant after translating $p$ by $b$ and converges strongly with a finite filtration on every target degree. Derived objects use the supplied columns; under DC, or supplied Cartan–Eilenberg comparison and homotopy data, it is natural in $K$ and independent of the resolution from $E_1$ onward.

For an additive left-exact $F$ and bounded-below $K$ with supplied Cartan–Eilenberg resolution $I$, there is a strongly convergent spectral sequence
$$E_2^{p,q}=R^pF(H^qK)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathbb R_I^{p+q}F(K),\qquad d_r:(p,q)\mapsto(p+r,q-r+1).$$
Its support is $p\ge0,q\ge b$ for a lower bound $b$ of $K$; translate $q$ by $b$ to obtain a first quadrant. The target has a finite decreasing filtration by resolution degree. With DC or supplied Cartan–Eilenberg comparisons and homotopies, the sequence is natural and independent of the resolution from $E_2$ onward.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be a field and $n\ge0$, let
$X=\mathbb P^n_k$ with dualizing line bundle $\omega_X=\mathcal O(-n-1)$ and
residue trace $t_X:H^n(X,\omega_X)\to k$
([[def-smooth-projective-dualizing-line-bundle-and-trace]]), and let
$\operatorname{Ext}^q_{\mathcal O_X}$ be the global sheaf Ext of
[[def-sheaf-ext-for-coherent-modules]].

1. **(The pairing.)** For every coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module $F$, every
   $q\in\{0,\dots,n\}$, $\alpha\in\operatorname{Ext}^{n-q}_{\mathcal O_X}(F,\omega_X)$
   and $\eta\in H^q(X,F)$ set
   $$\langle\alpha,\eta\rangle_F\;:=\;t_X\Bigl(\chi^n_{\omega_X}\bigl(\alpha\cdot\chi^q_F{}^{-1}(\eta)\bigr)\Bigr),$$
   where $\chi^q_F:\operatorname{Ext}^q_{\mathcal O_X}(\mathcal O_X,F)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^q(X,F)$
   is the canonical isomorphism of
   [[lem-injective-modules-flasque-and-ext-of-structure-sheaf]],
   $\chi^q_F{}^{-1}(\eta)$ is the corresponding class in
   $\operatorname{Ext}^q_{\mathcal O_X}(\mathcal O_X,F)$, and
   $\alpha\cdot\beta\in\operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathcal O_X}(\mathcal O_X,\omega_X)$
   is the Yoneda product of
   $\alpha\in\operatorname{Ext}^{n-q}_{\mathcal O_X}(F,\omega_X)$ with
   $\beta=\chi^q_F{}^{-1}(\eta)$, i.e. composition
   $\alpha\circ\beta$ of derived morphisms under
   $\operatorname{Ext}^{\bullet}_{\mathcal O_X}(-,-)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X))}(-,-[\bullet])$
   ([[thm-ext-is-hom-in-the-derived-category]],
   [[prop-yoneda-product-is-composition-in-the-derived-category]]). This
   **Serre duality pairing** is $k$-bilinear and natural in $F$.

2. **(Perfectness.)** For every coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module $F$ and every
   $q\in\{0,\dots,n\}$ the pairing
   $$\langle-,-\rangle_F:\operatorname{Ext}^{n-q}_{\mathcal O_X}(F,\omega_X)\times H^q(X,F)\longrightarrow k$$
   is a perfect pairing of $k$-vector spaces, i.e. both adjoint maps
   $\operatorname{Ext}^{n-q}_{\mathcal O_X}(F,\omega_X)\to H^q(X,F)^\vee$ and
   $H^q(X,F)\to\operatorname{Ext}^{n-q}_{\mathcal O_X}(F,\omega_X)^\vee$ are
   isomorphisms.

The case $q=n$ of clause 2 is the classical statement that
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_X}(F,\omega_X)\to H^n(X,F)^\vee$,
$\varphi\mapsto(\eta\mapsto t_X(H^n(\varphi)(\eta)))$, is an isomorphism, and
for $F=\mathcal O_X$ clause 2 recovers $H^{n-q}(X,\omega_X)\cong H^q(X,\mathcal O_X)^\vee$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a commutative
ring with $1$ ([[def-commutative-ring]]), let $n\ge0$, let $d\in\mathbb Z$ and
let $X=\mathbb P^n_A\cong\operatorname{Proj}A[x_0,\dots,x_n]$ be relative
projective space ([[def-relative-projective-space-standard-charts]],
[[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]]), with twisting sheaf
$\mathcal O_X(d)$ ([[def-twisting-sheaf-proj]]) and cohomology
$H^q(X,\mathcal O_X(d))$. Then
$$H^q(X,\mathcal O_X(d))=0\qquad\text{unless }q=0\text{ or }q=n.$$
If $n>0$, then $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))\cong A[x_0,\dots,x_n]_d$ when $d\ge0$
and $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))=0$ when $d<0$, where
$A[x_0,\dots,x_n]_d$ is the degree-$d$ graded piece
([[def-graded-ring-and-graded-module]]); and $H^n(X,\mathcal O_X(d))$ is the
free $A$-module on the Laurent monomials $x_0^{e_0}\cdots x_n^{e_n}$ with
$e_i<0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_ie_i=d$, so that it is nonzero precisely when
$d\le-n-1$ and $A\ne0$. For $n=0$ one has $\mathbb P^0_A=\operatorname{Spec}A$
and $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))\cong A$ for every $d\in\mathbb Z$, with all higher
groups zero. The zero ring $A=0$ is allowed: then $X=\varnothing$ and all
groups are zero, in agreement with both displayed descriptions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be a field and $n\ge0$, let
$S=k[x_0,\dots,x_n]$ be graded by total degree with $\deg x_i=1$, let
$\mathbb P^n_k=\operatorname{Proj}S$ with twisting sheaves
$\mathcal O(d)=\widetilde{S(d)}$, and let $F$ be a coherent
$\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^n_k}$-module. Then there is a finitely generated graded
$S$-module $M$ with $\widetilde M\cong F$ and an exact sequence of graded
$S$-modules with degree-preserving maps
$$0\longrightarrow F_{n+1}\longrightarrow F_n\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow F_0\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow 0$$
in which every $F_i$ is a finite direct sum of shifted free modules $S(d)$
with $d\in\mathbb Z$, and whose sheafification
$$0\longrightarrow\widetilde F_{n+1}\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow\widetilde F_0\longrightarrow F\longrightarrow 0$$
is an exact sequence of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^n_k}$-modules in which every
$\widetilde F_i$ is a finite direct sum $\bigoplus_j\mathcal O(d_{ij})$ of
twisting sheaves. The resolution has length at most $n+1$: the displayed free
terms $F_0,\dots,F_{n+1}$ are finite direct sums of shifted free modules, any
of them may be zero, a shorter resolution is allowed when it terminates
earlier, and the truncation degree of $M$ is chosen so that $M$ is finitely
generated and $\widetilde M\cong F$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) inherited from the finite
coherent-resolution and cohomological suppliers. Let $Y$ be smooth
quasi-projective over a field and $E$ a rank-$r$ bundle. For
$q:P=\mathbb P_{\mathrm{lines}}(E)\to Y$, $K^0(P)=G_0(P)$ is generated as a
$K^0(Y)$-module by $\mathcal O(a)$, $0\le a<r$. For $r\ge1$ and $a\ge0$,
$q_!\mathcal O(a)=\operatorname{Sym}^a(E^\vee)$. For $r=0$, the projective
bundle is empty, its $K$-groups and all $q_!\mathcal O(a)$ are zero, and the
assertion of generation is vacuous. This statement has the
corresponding dual form for quotient projective bundles.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R\to S$ be a local homomorphism of
Noetherian local rings, let $I\subsetneq R$ be an ideal, and let $M$ be a
finite $S$-module. If $M/IM$ is flat over $R/I$ and the multiplication map
$$I\otimes_R M\longrightarrow M$$
is injective, then $M$ is flat over $R$. There is **no** assumption that
$M$ is finitely generated as an $R$-module.
Every finitely generated torsion-free module over a principal ideal domain is finite free.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $I \trianglelefteq R$ satisfy $I \subseteq J(R)$, and let $M$ be a finitely generated left $R$-module. If $IM=M$, then $M=0$.

Assume AC and DC. On a regular Noetherian surface a coherent reflexive module is locally free. For a finite module $M$ over a normal Noetherian domain, a generic vector belonging to $M^{**}$ at every height-one localization belongs to $M^{**}$. For a coherent generic-rank-$r$ module on a regular surface, $(\wedge^rM)^{**}$ is the determinant line of $M^{**}$.

derivations.claim: Near a point of $L_\infty$, let $R$ be the regular local surface ring, $t$ a local equation of $L_\infty$, and $M$ the torsion-free stalk of $\mathcal E$. Multiplication by $t$ is injective on $M$. Lift a basis of $M/tM\cong(R/(t))^N$ to obtain a surjection $R^N\twoheadrightarrow M$ by Nakayama [F8]. If $K$ is its kernel, tensoring with $R/(t)$ is exact on the left because $t$ is injective on $M$; the lifted basis makes $(R/(t))^N\to M/tM$ an isomorphism, so $K/tK=0$. Nakayama [F8] gives $K=0$, proving local freeness of rank $N$ near the framed line.

Let $Q$ be the universal rank-two quotient bundle on the first factor. The section of $\mathcal O(1)$ on the second factor tensored with $Q$ on the first, induced by the second tautological line modulo the first, vanishes exactly on the diagonal. In affine coordinates transverse to the diagonal its two components are a regular parameter pair; hence its Koszul complex is exact and resolves $\mathcal O_\Delta$. Since $\det Q=\mathcal O(1)$ and $Q^*=\Omega^1(1)$, the resolution is $0\to\mathcal O(-1)\boxtimes\mathcal O(-2)\to\Omega^1(1)\boxtimes\mathcal O(-1)\to\mathcal O\boxtimes\mathcal O\to\mathcal O_\Delta\to0$. The regularity check is local along the diagonal, and outside it one component is a unit; this verifies exactness at every point. Its alternating $K$-class is the diagonal generator from [F5], but here the actual Koszul complex, rather than only its $K$-class, supplies the resolution.

The framing makes $\det\mathcal E$ trivial on $L_\infty$, so $c_1(\mathcal E)\cdot L_\infty=0$ and $\mu(\mathcal E)=0$. For a positive-rank subsheaf $\mathcal F\subset\mathcal E$, replace it by its saturation. At the generic point of $L_\infty$, use the chart $z_1\ne0$ with coordinates $x=z_0/z_1$, $y=z_2/z_1$; the local ring is $\mathbb C[x,y]_{(x)}$, a discrete valuation ring because every nonzero polynomial is a power of $x$ times a polynomial not divisible by $x$, and the latter is a unit after localization. Saturation makes both $\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal E/\mathcal F$ torsion-free there, hence free by [F7]. Thus reducing the inclusion modulo $x$ remains injective at that generic point. Taking the double dual of its top exterior power gives a morphism from the determinant line of $\mathcal F$ to the corresponding exterior power of $\mathcal E$ near the line; [F9] makes this extension a morphism across the finite non-locally-free set. It is nonzero at the generic point and therefore restricts to a nonzero map $\det(\mathcal F)|_{L_\infty}\to\bigwedge^{\mathrm{rk}\mathcal F}(W\otimes\mathcal O_{L_\infty})$. Some component into a trivial line bundle is a nonzero section of $(\det(\mathcal F)|_{L_\infty})^*$, forcing $\deg(\det(\mathcal F)|_{L_\infty})\le0$. This proves slope-semistability of $\mathcal E$ of slope zero.

A nonzero section of $\mathcal E(-d)$ for $d=1,2$ would give a rank-one subsheaf of $\mathcal E$ whose determinant has degree at least $d>0$, contrary to step 2.1. Hence $H^0(\mathcal E(-1))=H^0(\mathcal E(-2))=0$. A nonzero map $\mathcal E\to\mathcal O(-d)$ for $d=1,2$ would have a torsion-free image that is a quotient of $\mathcal E$ of slope at least zero: its kernel is a subsheaf of the slope-zero semistable sheaf, so has degree at most zero, while $\deg\mathcal E=0$. The same image is a subsheaf of $\mathcal O(-d)$ of degree at most $-d$. This is impossible. By coherent Serre duality [F4], these Hom vanishings give $H^2(\mathcal E(-1))=H^2(\mathcal E(-2))=0$.

The Hilbert polynomial gives $\chi(\mathcal E(-1))=\chi(\mathcal E(-2))=-k$. With the vanishings of step 3.1, $h^1(\mathcal E(-1))=h^1(\mathcal E(-2))=k$. The Euler sequence is locally split, so tensoring it by $\mathcal E$ remains exact; its first map therefore injects $H^0(\mathcal E\otimes\Omega^1)$ into $H^0(\mathcal E(-1))^3$, which is zero by step 3.1.

Serre duality identifies $H^2(\mathcal E\otimes\Omega^1)^*$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal E,T_{\mathbb P^2}(-3))$. The twisted Euler sequence is $0\to\mathcal O(-3-d)\to\mathcal O(-2-d)^3\to T_{\mathbb P^2}(-3-d)\to0$. For $d\ge-1$, both $H^0$ terms on the left vanish and $H^1(\mathcal O(-3-d))=0$ by [F5], hence $H^0(T_{\mathbb P^2}(-3-d))=0$. Any rank-one torsion-free subsheaf of $T_{\mathbb P^2}(-3)$ of degree at least $-1$ would extend by double dual to a nonzero map $\mathcal O(d)\to T_{\mathbb P^2}(-3)$ for some $d\ge-1$, a contradiction. Thus $T_{\mathbb P^2}(-3)$ is stable of slope $-3/2$. A nonzero map from the slope-zero semistable $\mathcal E$ to this stable sheaf would have image both a quotient of slope at least zero and a subsheaf of negative slope, impossible. Consequently $H^2(\mathcal E\otimes\Omega^1)=0$. From the Euler sequence and the Hilbert polynomial, $\chi(\mathcal E\otimes\Omega^1)=3\chi(\mathcal E(-1))-\chi(\mathcal E)=-(2k+N)$, so $h^1(\mathcal E\otimes\Omega^1)=2k+N$.

Tensor this resolution on its first factor by $\mathcal E(-1)$ and take derived pushforward to the second factor. The standard finite affine cover computes coherent cohomology by Čech [F5]; choose a Cartan–Eilenberg resolution of the resulting bounded complex. DC, obtained from AC by [F3], supplies compatible resolution comparisons. Filtering this one total complex in the two orders gives the first and second spectral sequences [F3]; the identity comparison of the total complex identifies their abutment and canonical edge maps. Thus no arbitrary splitting is used. By steps 3.1 and 5.1, all rows except $q=1$ vanish. The surviving row is $H^1(\mathcal E(-2))\mathcal O(-2)\to H^1(\mathcal E\otimes\Omega^1)\mathcal O(-1)\to H^1(\mathcal E(-1))\mathcal O$. Its only cohomology is $\mathcal E(-1)$ in the middle because the diagonal resolution transforms $\mathcal E(-1)$ to itself. Twisting by $\mathcal O(1)$ gives the displayed monad. The dimensions are exactly those from steps 4.1 and 5.1.

For a finite-type algebraic base $S$, tensor the relative diagonal Koszul resolution by the flat family and use the assumed base-change isomorphisms [A1]. The direct-image terms are vector bundles of ranks $k,2k+N,k$, and the finite filtered complex commutes with residue-field restriction. On every fiber, step 6.1 gives the monad. The right end map is surjective on every fiber, hence surjective by Nakayama [F8], and its kernel $K$ is locally free. Locally on $S$, write the remaining exact sequence as $0\to P^{-1}\to K\to\mathcal E\to0$, with $P^{-1}$ and $K$ flat over the base. Tensoring by any residue field $k(s)$ stays injective at the left because the fiber complex is a monad on the whole projective plane. Thus $\operatorname{Tor}_1^{\mathcal O_{S,s}}(k(s),\mathcal E)=0$, equivalently the maximal-ideal multiplication map is injective. Since $\mathcal E$ is finite over the local ring of $\mathbb P^2\times S$, [F6] proves flatness over $S$. The same base-change maps identify the relative middle cohomology with the given family. This is precisely the family range stated and does not assert base change outside it.

Fix integers $N\ge1$ and $k\ge0$ and standard Hermitian spaces $V=\mathbb C^k$, $W=\mathbb C^N$. A framed ADHM linear datum is $x=(B_1,B_2,I,J)$ with $B_i\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$, $I:W\to V$ and $J:V\to W$. Define the complex and real polynomial expressions

$$\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=[B_1,B_2]+IJ,\qquad \mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J.$$

The datum is stable if the vectors $B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w)$, with $m\ge0$, $i_j\in\{1,2\}$ and $w\in W$, span $V$. It is costable if there is no nonzero subspace of $V$ invariant under both $B_i$ and contained in $\ker J$. It is regular if it is stable and costable. The group $GL(V)$ acts by $g\cdot x=(gB_1g^{-1},gB_2g^{-1},gI,Jg^{-1})$. Its unitary subgroup is $U(V)$.

Write $X^s=\{x:\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=0,\ x\text{ stable}\}$, $X^{\mathrm{reg}}=\{x\in X^s:x\text{ costable}\}$ and, for real $\zeta\ge0$, $X_\zeta^U=\{x\in X^s:\mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=\zeta I_V\}$. Denote the corresponding orbit sets by $X^s/GL(V)$, $X^{\mathrm{reg}}/GL(V)$ and $X_\zeta^U/U(V)$, with quotient topologies when discussing their analytic spaces. A word frame consists of $k$ columns obtained by fixed words in $B_1,B_2$ applied to fixed standard basis vectors of $W$.

For $T_{\mathbb C}=(\mathbb C^*)^2\times(\mathbb C^*)^N$, write $t_1,t_2,e_1,\ldots,e_N$ for the coordinate characters and put $h=\operatorname{diag}(e_1^{-1},\ldots,e_N^{-1})$. Its action is $(t_1,t_2,h)\cdot x=(t_1B_1,t_2B_2,Ih^{-1},t_1t_2hJ)$. The compact torus is its subgroup on which all characters have modulus one. The framing representation thus has character $\sum_\alpha e_\alpha^{-1}$ and its dual has character $\sum_\alpha e_\alpha$.

These are finite-dimensional matrix definitions. They do not assert a real/complex quotient correspondence, a sheaf or ASD identification, or a noncompact pushforward. In particular, positive-FI stability and zero-FI regularity are distinct conditions; neither an endpoint identification nor an ordinary ASD interpretation follows from this definition.

Assume AC. Fix $N\ge1$, $k\ge0$, $V=\mathbb C^k$ and $W=\mathbb C^N$ with their standard bases. Let $X$ be the stable locus in the complex ADHM equation $[B_1,B_2]+IJ=0$, where $B_i\in\operatorname{End}(V)$, $I:W\to V$, $J:V\to W$, and stability means that the vectors $B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w)$ span $V$. The action $g\cdot(B_1,B_2,I,J)=(gB_1g^{-1},gB_2g^{-1},gI,Jg^{-1})$ of $GL(V)$ on $X$ is free and proper. Its orbit quotient with quotient topology is a Hausdorff second-countable complex manifold of complex dimension $2kN$, with tangent space $\ker d_1/\operatorname{im}d_0$ for the infinitesimal ADHM deformation maps.

For $k>0$, a word frame $C(x)$ is a matrix whose columns are $k$ fixed words in $B_1,B_2$ applied to fixed standard framing basis vectors. The opens $U_C=\{x:\det C(x)\ne0\}$ cover $X$; words of length at most $k-1$ suffice. Each slice $S_C=\{x\in U_C:C(x)=I_V\}$ gives quotient coordinates, with $GL(V)\times S_C\to U_C$ a biholomorphism. Slice changes are holomorphic, in fact given by matrix inversion and polynomial operations on their domains. The quotient is also a separated smooth finite-type complex algebraic variety with a finite $T$-invariant affine atlas of these slices, and the map from $X$ is a geometric quotient in the regular-function sense.

Let $T=(S^1)^2\times(S^1)^N$ act by $(t_1,t_2,h)\cdot(B_1,B_2,I,J)=(t_1B_1,t_2B_2,Ih^{-1},t_1t_2hJ)$, with $h$ acting on the $\alpha$th standard framing vector by $e_\alpha^{-1}$. This descends to a smooth holomorphic action. At any fixed quotient point represented by $x$, there is a unique $g(t)\in GL(V)$ with $t\cdot x=g(t)\cdot x$. If column $\ell$ of $C(x)$ uses framing color $\alpha_\ell$ and contains $a_\ell,b_\ell$ letters $B_1,B_2$, then

$$g(t)=C(x)\operatorname{diag}(e_{\alpha_\ell}t_1^{a_\ell}t_2^{b_\ell})C(x)^{-1}.$$

Thus the lift is a smooth character representation, without assuming Zariski density or a GIT linearization theorem. For $k=0$ the quotient is a point and these matrices and tangent spaces have their empty-dimensional interpretations. No correspondence with a real moment-map quotient, sheaf moduli or ASD connections is asserted.

Assume AC. Let $L_\infty=\{z_0=0\}\subset\mathbb P^2_{\mathbb C}$ and let $\mathcal E$ be a torsion-free algebraic coherent sheaf (a locally finitely presented module over the structure sheaf) of generic rank $N\ge1$. Torsion-free means that no nonzero stalk element is annihilated by a nonzero local function. Suppose it has a framing, namely an isomorphism $\phi:\mathcal E|_{L_\infty}\xrightarrow{\sim}W\otimes\mathcal O_{L_\infty}$ for $W=\mathbb C^N$, and Hilbert polynomial $\chi(\mathcal E(m))=N\binom{m+2}{2}-k$ for $k\ge0$, where $\chi$ is the alternating sum of coherent-sheaf cohomology dimensions. Then $\mathcal E$ is locally free near $L_\infty$ and

$$H^0(\mathcal E(-1))=H^0(\mathcal E(-2))=H^2(\mathcal E(-1))=H^2(\mathcal E(-2))=0.$$

$$\dim H^1(\mathcal E(-1))=\dim H^1(\mathcal E(-2))=k,\qquad H^0(\mathcal E\otimes\Omega^1)=H^2(\mathcal E\otimes\Omega^1)=0,\qquad \dim H^1(\mathcal E\otimes\Omega^1)=2k+N.$$
The diagonal on $\mathbb P^2\times\mathbb P^2$ has its length-two Koszul resolution from the regular rank-two section described in the proof. Its associated finite Beilinson hypercohomology complex, applied to $\mathcal E(-1)$ and twisted by $\mathcal O(1)$, is a monad

$$H^1(\mathcal E(-2))\otimes\mathcal O(-1)\longrightarrow H^1(\mathcal E\otimes\Omega^1)\otimes\mathcal O\longrightarrow H^1(\mathcal E(-1))\otimes\mathcal O(1)$$

whose only cohomology is $\mathcal E$ in the middle. For an algebraic family over a finite-type complex base, the same construction is a family of monads provided the sheaf is flat over the base, the displayed cohomology groups have the stated constant ranks, and the corresponding cohomology-and-base-change maps are isomorphisms.

Assume AC. Fix $N\ge1$, $k\ge0$, standard Hermitian $V=\mathbb C^k$, $W=\mathbb C^N$ and ADHM data $x=(B_1,B_2,I,J)$ with the complex equation $[B_1,B_2]+IJ=0$. Stability means that the $B_1,B_2$ words applied to $I(W)$ span $V$; costability means no nonzero common invariant subspace of $V$ lies in $\ker J$; regular means both. Set

$$\mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J.$$

For every $\zeta>0$, each stable $GL(V)$ orbit meets $\mu_{\mathbb R}=\zeta I_V$ in exactly one $U(V)$ orbit, and the inclusion induces a diffeomorphism of smooth real manifolds

$$\{\mu_{\mathbb C}=0,\ \mu_{\mathbb R}=\zeta I_V,\ \mathrm{stable}\}/U(V)\ \cong\ X^s/GL(V).$$

At $\zeta=0$, every stable datum satisfying the real equation is automatically costable. Each regular complex orbit meets the zero real level in exactly one unitary orbit, giving instead

$$\{\mu_{\mathbb C}=0,\ \mu_{\mathbb R}=0,\ \mathrm{stable}\}/U(V)\ \cong\ X^{\mathrm{reg}}/GL(V).$$

Both identifications are equivariant for the compact rotation/framing torus in the raw-data convention. For $k=0$ all spaces are points. This theorem identifies the stated finite-dimensional quotients; it asserts no correspondence with sheaves or ASD connections, and no identification of the entire positive-FI quotient with the zero-FI regular locus.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be a field and $n\ge0$, let
$X=\mathbb P^n_k$ with dualizing line bundle $\omega_X=\mathcal O(-n-1)$ and
residue trace $t_X:H^n(X,\omega_X)\to k$
([[def-smooth-projective-dualizing-line-bundle-and-trace]]), and let
$\operatorname{Ext}^q_{\mathcal O_X}$ be the global sheaf Ext of
[[def-sheaf-ext-for-coherent-modules]].

1. **(The pairing.)** For every coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module $F$, every
   $q\in\{0,\dots,n\}$, $\alpha\in\operatorname{Ext}^{n-q}_{\mathcal O_X}(F,\omega_X)$
   and $\eta\in H^q(X,F)$ set
   $$\langle\alpha,\eta\rangle_F\;:=\;t_X\Bigl(\chi^n_{\omega_X}\bigl(\alpha\cdot\chi^q_F{}^{-1}(\eta)\bigr)\Bigr),$$
   where $\chi^q_F:\operatorname{Ext}^q_{\mathcal O_X}(\mathcal O_X,F)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^q(X,F)$
   is the canonical isomorphism of
   [[lem-injective-modules-flasque-and-ext-of-structure-sheaf]],
   $\chi^q_F{}^{-1}(\eta)$ is the corresponding class in
   $\operatorname{Ext}^q_{\mathcal O_X}(\mathcal O_X,F)$, and
   $\alpha\cdot\beta\in\operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathcal O_X}(\mathcal O_X,\omega_X)$
   is the Yoneda product of
   $\alpha\in\operatorname{Ext}^{n-q}_{\mathcal O_X}(F,\omega_X)$ with
   $\beta=\chi^q_F{}^{-1}(\eta)$, i.e. composition
   $\alpha\circ\beta$ of derived morphisms under
   $\operatorname{Ext}^{\bullet}_{\mathcal O_X}(-,-)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X))}(-,-[\bullet])$
   ([[thm-ext-is-hom-in-the-derived-category]],
   [[prop-yoneda-product-is-composition-in-the-derived-category]]). This
   **Serre duality pairing** is $k$-bilinear and natural in $F$.

2. **(Perfectness.)** For every coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module $F$ and every
   $q\in\{0,\dots,n\}$ the pairing
   $$\langle-,-\rangle_F:\operatorname{Ext}^{n-q}_{\mathcal O_X}(F,\omega_X)\times H^q(X,F)\longrightarrow k$$
   is a perfect pairing of $k$-vector spaces, i.e. both adjoint maps
   $\operatorname{Ext}^{n-q}_{\mathcal O_X}(F,\omega_X)\to H^q(X,F)^\vee$ and
   $H^q(X,F)\to\operatorname{Ext}^{n-q}_{\mathcal O_X}(F,\omega_X)^\vee$ are
   isomorphisms.

The case $q=n$ of clause 2 is the classical statement that
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_X}(F,\omega_X)\to H^n(X,F)^\vee$,
$\varphi\mapsto(\eta\mapsto t_X(H^n(\varphi)(\eta)))$, is an isomorphism, and
for $F=\mathcal O_X$ clause 2 recovers $H^{n-q}(X,\omega_X)\cong H^q(X,\mathcal O_X)^\vee$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a commutative
ring with $1$ ([[def-commutative-ring]]), let $n\ge0$, let $d\in\mathbb Z$ and
let $X=\mathbb P^n_A\cong\operatorname{Proj}A[x_0,\dots,x_n]$ be relative
projective space ([[def-relative-projective-space-standard-charts]],
[[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]]), with twisting sheaf
$\mathcal O_X(d)$ ([[def-twisting-sheaf-proj]]) and cohomology
$H^q(X,\mathcal O_X(d))$. Then
$$H^q(X,\mathcal O_X(d))=0\qquad\text{unless }q=0\text{ or }q=n.$$
If $n>0$, then $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))\cong A[x_0,\dots,x_n]_d$ when $d\ge0$
and $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))=0$ when $d<0$, where
$A[x_0,\dots,x_n]_d$ is the degree-$d$ graded piece
([[def-graded-ring-and-graded-module]]); and $H^n(X,\mathcal O_X(d))$ is the
free $A$-module on the Laurent monomials $x_0^{e_0}\cdots x_n^{e_n}$ with
$e_i<0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_ie_i=d$, so that it is nonzero precisely when
$d\le-n-1$ and $A\ne0$. For $n=0$ one has $\mathbb P^0_A=\operatorname{Spec}A$
and $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))\cong A$ for every $d\in\mathbb Z$, with all higher
groups zero. The zero ring $A=0$ is allowed: then $X=\varnothing$ and all
groups are zero, in agreement with both displayed descriptions.
The field $\mathbb C$ is algebraically closed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

For a nonzero Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak m,k)$ the following are equivalent: $R$ is regular; $\operatorname{pd}_Rk<\infty$; $\operatorname{gldim}R<\infty$; and every finite $R$-module has finite projective dimension. When these hold, $\operatorname{gldim}R=\operatorname{pd}_Rk=\dim R$. A nonzero finite module over regular local $R$ is maximal Cohen–Macaulay (depth $\dim R$) if and only if it is free.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R\to S$ be a local homomorphism of
Noetherian local rings, let $I\subsetneq R$ be an ideal, and let $M$ be a
finite $S$-module. If $M/IM$ is flat over $R/I$ and the multiplication map
$$I\otimes_R M\longrightarrow M$$
is injective, then $M$ is flat over $R$. There is **no** assumption that
$M$ is finitely generated as an $R$-module.

derivations.claim: Direct multiplication gives $\beta\alpha=(-z_0B_2+z_2)(z_0B_1-z_1)+(z_0B_1-z_1)(z_0B_2-z_2)+z_0^2IJ=z_0^2([B_1,B_2]+IJ)=0$. The $z_0z_1$ and $z_0z_2$ cross terms cancel pairwise, and the $z_1z_2$ terms cancel. On $L_\infty$, $\alpha=(-z_1,-z_2,0)^T$ is injective at every point because $z_1,z_2$ are not simultaneously zero. Thus $\alpha$ has full rank generically; its sheaf kernel is a torsion subsheaf of the locally free source, and hence is zero.

Conversely, let $\mathcal E$ be a framed torsion-free sheaf with the stated Hilbert polynomial. The preceding Beilinson lemma constructs its monad, with terms $V_1\mathcal O(-1)$, $M\mathcal O$, and $V_2\mathcal O(1)$ of ranks $k,2k+N,k$. Its restriction to $L_\infty$ remains exact at the ends because $\mathcal E$ is locally free there. Put $K=\ker\beta|_{L_\infty}$. The sequence $0\to V_1\mathcal O(-1)\to K\to W\mathcal O\to0$ splits since $\operatorname{Ext}^1(W\mathcal O,V_1\mathcal O(-1))=V_1\otimes W^*\otimes H^1(\mathcal O(-1))=0$.

At a point of $L_\infty$, $\beta=(z_2,-z_1,0)$ is onto. At an affine point $[1:u_1:u_2]$, failure of surjectivity would give a nonzero $\lambda\in V^*$ with $\lambda B_1=u_1\lambda$, $\lambda B_2=u_2\lambda$, and $\lambda I=0$. Then $\lambda$ annihilates every vector $B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w)$, contradicting stability. Hence $\beta$ is everywhere onto, so $K=\ker\beta$ is a vector bundle of rank $k+N$.

A fiber kernel of $\alpha$ over $[1:u_1:u_2]$ is a nonzero vector $v$ with $B_1v=u_1v$, $B_2v=u_2v$, and $Jv=0$. Each $u_i$ must be an eigenvalue of the fixed matrix $B_i$, so the rank-drop locus is contained in the finite product of the two finite spectra. Such a vector spans a common invariant line in $\ker J$, so costability fails. Conversely, if costability fails, choose a nonzero common invariant subspace $S\subseteq\ker J$. On $S$, the complex equation implies $[B_1,B_2]|_S=-IJ|_S=0$, so the restrictions commute. By [F6] they have a common eigenvector; its eigenvalues give an affine point where $\alpha$ has a fiber kernel. Therefore $\alpha$ has full fiber rank everywhere exactly for costable data.

The remaining line extension $0\to V_1\mathcal O(-1)\oplus W\mathcal O\to M\mathcal O\to V_2\mathcal O(1)\to0$ has class in $\operatorname{Hom}(V_2,V_1)\otimes H^1(\mathcal O(-2))$, since $H^1(\mathcal O(-1))=0$. Twist by $\mathcal O(-1)$ and take cohomology. The connecting map $V_2\to V_1\otimes H^1(\mathcal O(-2))$ is an isomorphism: the adjacent groups $H^0(\mathcal O(-1))$ and $H^1(\mathcal O(-1))$ vanish, while $H^1(\mathcal O(-2))\cong\mathbb C$. Thus $V_2$ is identified with $V_1$ by this canonical extension class. Choosing a basis of $V_1$ and using the fixed framed basis of $W$ identifies $M=V\oplus V\oplus W$ and the line maps with the two Euler blocks in the Statement. Any other such choice differs by one simultaneous element of $GL(V)$.

The sequence $0\to V\mathcal O(-1)\xrightarrow{\alpha}K\to\mathcal E\to0$ has locally free first two terms. Away from the finite rank-drop set of step 2.2, $\mathcal E$ is locally free; hence any torsion is supported at finitely many points. At such a point, the local ring is regular of dimension two and this sequence gives $\operatorname{pd}\mathcal E\le1$. The Auslander–Buchsbaum formula [F7] gives $\operatorname{depth}\mathcal E\ge1$. A nonzero finite-length torsion submodule would force depth zero, so no such torsion exists. Thus $\mathcal E$ is torsion-free of rank $(2k+N)-k-k=N$. The rank drops only off $L_\infty$, so $\mathcal E$ is locally free near the framing line.

The remaining coefficients of the two linear maps are their $z_0$ coefficients, so write $\alpha=(z_0B_1-z_1,z_0B_2-z_2,z_0J)^T$ and $\beta=(-z_0C_1+z_2,z_0C_2-z_1,z_0I)$. The coefficients of $z_0z_1$ and $z_0z_2$ in $\beta\alpha=0$ force $C_1=B_2$ and $C_2=B_1$; the $z_0^2$ coefficient is then $[B_1,B_2]+IJ=0$. This recovers the stated ADHM form. The surjectivity of $\beta$ implies stability: if $U=\operatorname{span}\{B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(W)\}$ were proper, it is invariant and the induced $B_1,B_2$ on $V/U$ commute because $[B_1,B_2]=-IJ$ has image in $U$. Their dual actions on the nonzero annihilator $U^\perp\subset V^*$ commute, so [F6] gives a common eigen-covector $\lambda\ne0$ with $\lambda I=0$. At the corresponding affine point, $\lambda\beta=0$, contradicting surjectivity.

On $L_\infty$, the complex is $0\to V\mathcal O_{L_\infty}(-1)\xrightarrow{(-z_1,-z_2,0)^T}(V\oplus V\oplus W)\mathcal O_{L_\infty}\xrightarrow{(z_2,-z_1,0)}V\mathcal O_{L_\infty}(1)\to0$. The first two $V$ summands form the Euler resolution of the zero sheaf on the line, while the $W$ summand passes unchanged to middle cohomology. The framing is therefore the canonical identification $\mathcal E|_{L_\infty}=W\otimes\mathcal O_{L_\infty}$. In the Grothendieck group, the monad gives $[\mathcal E]=[(V\oplus V\oplus W)\mathcal O]-[V\mathcal O(-1)]-[V\mathcal O(1)]$. Taking Euler characteristics after twisting by $\mathcal O(m)$ and using $\chi(\mathcal O(d))=\binom{d+2}{2}$ yields $\chi(\mathcal E(m))=N\binom{m+2}{2}-k$.

The Beilinson construction is natural under framed sheaf isomorphisms, so an isomorphism of framed sheaves induces maps on the cohomology vector spaces used in steps 1.2–6.2 and hence a single change of basis $g\in GL(V)$; the normalized Euler blocks force the recovered tuples to differ by $g\cdot(B_1,B_2,I,J)$. Conversely such a $g$ is an isomorphism of monads acting trivially on $W$, and therefore induces a framed sheaf isomorphism. This proves the pointwise inverse equivalence modulo $GL(V)$. For a finite-type data family, step 2.1 makes $\beta$ surjective on the total space, so $K=\ker\beta$ is locally free. The sequence $0\to V\mathcal O(-1)\to K\to\mathcal E\to0$ is exact and its terms before $\mathcal E$ are flat over the base. After tensoring with any residue field of the base, the first map remains sheaf-injective by step 1.1; hence $\operatorname{Tor}_1(k(s),\mathcal E)=0$. Since $\mathcal E$ is finite over each local ring of $\mathbb P^2\times S$ and its residue fiber is a vector space over the residue field, [F8] gives flatness over $S$. Under the stated relative cohomology and base-change hypotheses, the same constructions use vector bundles and are inverse for families.

Step 2.2 proves that costability is equivalent to fiberwise injectivity of $\alpha$. Since $\beta$ is surjective and $K$ is locally free, the quotient $K/\operatorname{im}\alpha$ is locally free exactly when $\alpha$ has constant full rank; failure at any point gives a fiber dimension jump. Hence the locally-free sheaf locus is precisely the regular ADHM locus. Combining this with [F4] gives the positive-FI and zero-FI identifications in the Statement.

Apply the family equivalence to $S=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$. A first-order deformation of the ADHM data is $(\dot B_1,\dot B_2,\dot I,\dot J)$ satisfying $d\mu_{\mathbb C}=0$; infinitesimal changes of basis are $d_0(\xi)=([\xi,B_1],[\xi,B_2],\xi I,-J\xi)$. Differentiating the monad gives the chain perturbation $(\dot\alpha,\dot\beta)$ with $\beta\dot\alpha+\dot\beta\alpha=0$, and a change by $d_0(\xi)$ is the corresponding chain homotopy. Since the family construction and its inverse commute with this dual-number base change, they induce inverse linear maps on first-order framed deformations and on the quotient tangent spaces $\ker d_1/\operatorname{im}d_0$.

Let the rotation torus act on homogeneous coordinates with characters $1,t_1,t_2$, and let $h=\operatorname{diag}(e_1^{-1},\ldots,e_N^{-1})$ act on $W$. On the monad vector spaces choose characters $V(t_1t_2)^{-1}$ in the source, $Vt_2^{-1}\oplus Vt_1^{-1}\oplus Wh$ in the middle, and $V$ in the target, with the natural linearizations of $\mathcal O(-1)$ and $\mathcal O(1)$. The first and second blocks are equivariant because the ratios of middle to source characters are respectively $t_1,t_2$; the $J$ block has ratio $t_1t_2h$; in $\beta$, the first two ratios are $t_2,t_1$ and the framing block ratio is $h^{-1}$. These are exactly the raw transformations in [F1]. On $L_\infty$ the Euler blocks cancel, leaving the framing factor $Wh$; its character is $\sum_a e_a^{-1}$ and its dual has character $\sum_a e_a$. Thus the monad correspondence is torus-equivariant in the specified dual-framing convention.

If $k=0$, $V=0$, all four maps and both equations are the unique zero-dimensional maps, stability and costability are vacuous, and the monad is $0\to W\mathcal O\to0$. Its middle cohomology is the framed bundle $W\mathcal O$ with Hilbert polynomial $N\binom{m+2}{2}$. Conversely, [F3] constructs this same zero-term monad from every framed sheaf with that polynomial, so the framing identifies each such sheaf with $W\mathcal O$. Thus both moduli spaces are points, and all empty-matrix and Euler-block conventions are satisfied.

$$\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=[B_1,B_2]+IJ,\qquad \mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J.$$

The datum is stable if the vectors $B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w)$, with $m\ge0$, $i_j\in\{1,2\}$ and $w\in W$, span $V$. It is costable if there is no nonzero subspace of $V$ invariant under both $B_i$ and contained in $\ker J$. It is regular if it is stable and costable. The group $GL(V)$ acts by $g\cdot x=(gB_1g^{-1},gB_2g^{-1},gI,Jg^{-1})$. Its unitary subgroup is $U(V)$.

Write $X^s=\{x:\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=0,\ x\text{ stable}\}$, $X^{\mathrm{reg}}=\{x\in X^s:x\text{ costable}\}$ and, for real $\zeta\ge0$, $X_\zeta^U=\{x\in X^s:\mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=\zeta I_V\}$. Denote the corresponding orbit sets by $X^s/GL(V)$, $X^{\mathrm{reg}}/GL(V)$ and $X_\zeta^U/U(V)$, with quotient topologies when discussing their analytic spaces. A word frame consists of $k$ columns obtained by fixed words in $B_1,B_2$ applied to fixed standard basis vectors of $W$.

For $T_{\mathbb C}=(\mathbb C^*)^2\times(\mathbb C^*)^N$, write $t_1,t_2,e_1,\ldots,e_N$ for the coordinate characters and put $h=\operatorname{diag}(e_1^{-1},\ldots,e_N^{-1})$. Its action is $(t_1,t_2,h)\cdot x=(t_1B_1,t_2B_2,Ih^{-1},t_1t_2hJ)$. The compact torus is its subgroup on which all characters have modulus one. The framing representation thus has character $\sum_\alpha e_\alpha^{-1}$ and its dual has character $\sum_\alpha e_\alpha$.

These are finite-dimensional matrix definitions. They do not assert a real/complex quotient correspondence, a sheaf or ASD identification, or a noncompact pushforward. In particular, positive-FI stability and zero-FI regularity are distinct conditions; neither an endpoint identification nor an ordinary ASD interpretation follows from this definition.

At $\zeta=0$, every stable datum satisfying the real equation is automatically costable. Each regular complex orbit meets the zero real level in exactly one unitary orbit, giving instead
